utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic and Cynthia Dresden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I hope you all had a nice weekend and you are fully energised to carry on and finish with this witness. Any preliminaries before we start?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, only this: Professor Shoup asked if he could have a copy of the document that I showed him on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P1275 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. Your Honour, we considered the matter over the weekend, and in fact it is, of course, a public document because it was made an exhibit. So although I think it's right to say that exhibits aren't publicly put out as quickly as transcripts, nonetheless, I see no reason why he shouldn't have a copy, and we'll provide him or Mr. Ackerman can provide him with a copy when he's finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Anything from your side, Mr. Ackerman? No. So I think we can -- usher, please, could you escort Professor Shoup. Do you think you will finish today, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope so, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be proceeding with the cross-examination this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And hopefully conclude with your evidence so you can return back home. I hope you had a restful weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are energised. Doesn't mean to say that entitles you to prolong your answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I understand. I understand that. I'll try to be to the point, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please to be as precise and concise as possible, otherwise I'm afraid you will still be here tomorrow. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Korner: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, I want to ask you this morning to begin with a little bit about the sources that you have relied so heavily upon for your report; namely, the NWID report and "Balkan Battlegrounds."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The NWID report was commissioned by the Dutch government. Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Commissioned as a result of the criticism it had received for its role in the events of Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also because, in fact, some charges had been brought against some members of the military in a Dutch court?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I'm not aware of. But I'm sure that's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this right, and if you don't know the answer please say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the report looked at three aspects of these events. First of all, Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not read the parts on Srebrenica because of a shortage of time. This interests me greatly what their conclusions are, but yes I'm aware of that part of the report as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So you have never read the part of Srebrenica under Tito?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, I'm sorry. Srebrenica under Tito, yes, but not the part about the siege of Srebrenica itself. I didn't get to that because of a lack of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It actually runs to about 6.000 pages?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you only read parts of the report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read those parts which seemed relevant to this trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also looked at national politics, that is to say, the Dutch political outlook at that period?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally at UN politics?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of this, that one of the problems that the authors of this report faced was that they could not get access to many of the original documents, the sources?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, but I am aware of the fact that they relied heavily on secondary sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were actually refused permission to look at the archives in Belgrade. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I may have read that at some point. As I said a minute ago, I was struck by the fact that they relied on secondary sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Duijzings, upon whom you rely heavily -- and this is not meant of any criticism as I have no doubt at all that he is an extremely well-regarded academic, but he is in fact an anthropologist, isn't he, not a historian?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can I turn next to "Balkan Battlegrounds." That is -- or the two volumes are the CIA's discussion, as it were, of open-source material?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They say that. I remain convinced that probably their knowledge of the war was acquired by aerial surveillance and these kinds of things they can't put in the book influenced their conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this that somewhere in your report, but you don't know, that, do you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why did you say something that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you agree that there is nothing in that report, as it says, that is -- that covers anything outside open-source material?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. I don't agree entirely because there are conclusions such as those that I quote in the volume that appear to me to be based on material that is not only open, but perhaps not available to us. I will give the example of that statement about the VRS being in control of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 306, is that it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the one that Mr. Ackerman referred you to.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree, nobody else has a copy of this, but it's the one that was read to you. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Final analysis, Mr. Ackerman more or less towards the end of your examination-in-chief read you the passage that the Bosnian Serb army undertook these ethnic cleansing operations because it believed the Muslim population posed an armed threat, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. You said -- you referred me to the -- your answer was: "I don't agree entirely because there are conclusions such as those I quote in the volume that appear to me to be based on material that is not only open, but perhaps not available to us. I will give the example of that statement about the VRS being in control of ethnic cleansing." Now, were you referring to that statement? Perhaps you'd like to have a look at the book?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is getting a little confusing. If you don't mind, I think I better take a look at what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let me say simply that I don't -- so far, I don't see an inconsistency. I don't agree always with the conclusions of the CIA. I assume that when they make a sweeping judgement, as they do -- I believe here that that sweeping judgement is based on a knowledge that covers both open and closed sources. That's really where I stand, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that's where you stand. You have to stand there, don't you, Professor Shoup, because effectively you are relying heavily on these two reports as the only source material that you have looked at effectively since your book?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In doing research for this project, I looked for new source materials, and then focussed on these materials because I thought they were written with a great deal of authority and knowledge of the Bosnian situation. Other things, I don't quote. I'll give you the example of Professor Gow's book in which I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause because I'm going to come that book.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the third matter I want to ask you about. But please, you told us that you were greatly cheered, and I'm paraphrasing, to see that "Balkan Battlegrounds" supported what you and Professor Burg had written?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the sense that I didn't see any flagrant mistakes that we had made in our volume, and we had very little to go on except our own research resources, and apparently the CIA, with its vast resources, didn't seem to contradict specifically what we had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, could you give the witness the one and only copy of this book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at the passage that was quoted to you at page 306.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see, 306. Are we talking about final analysis?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the part that talks about --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Bosnian Serb army undertook ethnic cleansing," and so forth? Now what is the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The question is, is there any source quoted for that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a footnote 25. If that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I have it back.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is going to be a follow-up on this question, Ms. Korner, perhaps you could have the page photocopied so that we can follow, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, it is a Defence exhibit. I'll tell you the number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it part of the Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment -- as I said, at the end of this, I'm going to object to these books. I know Mr. Ackerman has listed it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean if it is intended to be a Defence exhibit and has been given to us, then perhaps we can have a look at it, and you don't need to photocopy it. Which number was it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll have it in just a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at the footnote that is referred to on the next page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can do copies of it, of course, Your Honours. It's probably simpler. Can I -- I think the simplest thing is, so that Your Honours can see this. I'll ask the usher -- I'll move on to another topic -- ask the usher to copy pages 306, 307, and then the following 308 and 309. And at the moment, it's part of what Mr. Ackerman has called DB372.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. 2, according to Ms. Gustin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's DB373, page 306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I have as well. Anyway, photocopy that, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while that's happening --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all those pages are an exhibit. There's no need to go off and photocopy them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner said 306 to 309. We only have up to 307 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have 306, 307, 308 and 309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have -- oh, yeah, there is 308 is footnotes or end notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And 309 is notes. So you've have got all four pages. They don't need to be copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 308 is -- I can't read anything on the photocopy that I have. Because all black, at least one half of the page. Yes, in the meantime, I think we can follow from -- on the basis of what we have, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The book's now gone, Your Honour. It doesn't matter anyhow. I want to move on to another aspect and I'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what you said about Professor Gow who, as you've told the Court on a number of occasions, gave evidence for the Prosecution in the Tadic trial. And while we're on that, I think Professor -- if he is a professor -- what's the name of the -- Hayden gave evidence for the Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were listed as a witness but not actually called.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 32, you said this, of the LiveNote from the 5th of February --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner said something like, Professor Hayden, if he is a professor? Does the Prosecution have any evidence to suggest that he's not a professor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This witness has told you -- has told the Prosecutor he is a professor. She's now suggesting to you that he may not be. I wonder if she has a basis for that. It's like the other day when she told you that review came from the New York Times. I wonder if she has a basis for that, too. She is telling you things and suggesting things to you that I think she has no basis for, and I think that's totally improper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was actually because I wasn't sure. I'm not suggesting, I can't remember whether he was a professor or a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What nationality is he? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's an American. I'm sorry, if he has told me that he is a professor, of course I accept that. I have simply forgotten. I think Mr. Ackerman is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's go ahead. Of course, I mean, I do understand Mr. Ackerman's preoccupation because here in Europe you can be a professor even if you're teaching primary school --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Believe you me, Mr. Ackerman -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I wasn't suggesting that he isn't a professor. I just had forgotten whether or not he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can assure you that if I'm going to suggest something, I will make it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have now lost the note I wanted to make. Sorry, Your Honour, I wrote down in my note page 32 of the LiveNote -- yes, here we are. I've got it, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's at page 32 of the LiveNote of the 5th of February. You said the second new source of great importance is the two-volume study by the CIA called "Balkan Battlegrounds", and the third is a book by Gow on -- it's actually called "The Serbian Project." "It simply didn't work as well as I had thought." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Gow has said that he would really dot the i's and cross the t's and show us exactly how Belgrade directed the VRS and the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the implication that he would have new materials. I didn't see the new materials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you check all of the materials that he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I read the -- his text. I didn't go to his footnotes. I was obviously presuming that he would present new evidence in the text that might help us understand the relationship between Belgrade and the VRS and the SDS. And rightly or wrongly, I felt that it wasn't much help in that respect. You know, I don't want to dismiss this entirely but...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. But his thesis runs counter to yours, doesn't it? He, in fact, in terms asserts that many of the operations were directed from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he counters perhaps -- on the other hand, he also says, which I thought was interesting, that Mladic operated very much on his own. This is exactly what the CIA said. He only gave examples of the intervention of the Serb army in Bosnia that seemed really to be the opposite of this case. That is, for example, when the Muslim forces reach the Drina River, he cites this as a one very prominent example of the Serbian intervention in the war. The Bosnian forces reached the Drina River. They mortar across the Drina River to the Serb side. And lo and behold, the Serb army answers back. I'm sympathetic to what Professor Gow is trying to do. If there's evidence that we need to know, I'd like to know it. I'm not partial in this sense but I felt those examples were not good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you agree that he footnotes for his assertions, and you haven't checked those footnotes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no need if the assertions themselves such as mortaring across the Drina River are well known and don't seem to back up his thesis, I'm not going to pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to move to something else that you said on the 5th of February.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 37 of the LiveNote, you said that -- when you were asked the question of Greater Serbia, it was put to you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the questions that has been contended here in this Tribunal since its beginning was the question of whether or not an effort was being made to create what is referred to as a Greater Serbia. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said sure, of course. I think first there is some -- there is a need to be cautious about the use of the term. The Serbs never themselves laid out a plan for a Greater Serbia. I want you to have a look, please, at another document, P20. P20, please. This is the minutes of a meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party on the 15th of October. I take it you've never seen that before?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you remember the 15th of October is the day of the walkout?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is a discussion of the minutes of the party council held on the premises of the deputies club on the 15th of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you turn to Mr. -- It's page 2 of the translation, Mr. Ekmecic.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Him, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where he talks about the upcoming plebiscite that's going to be held, that the contact should be continued for the search for a political solution, the Serbs have created regions which are not connected --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and these regions must not be allowed to establish their governments which would not be connected. In public we must let it be known that we can set up a Serbian government with its seat in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly, Madam Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought somebody behind me said slow down, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This evening, we must get rid of the illusion that a form of life together with the Muslims and Croats can be found. And then if we go on, please, to -- we see that Mr. Milanovic, sorry, Mr. Ostojic, Karadzic spoke. Can you come, please, to the fourth page in translation where Radovan Neskovic speaks.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neskovic, Radovan Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "Since they will not revoke their decisions, I suggest that a parliamentary crisis be provoked. Demand new elections, because in this way we would gain time which suits us. As regards outvoting, we were the first to use it at the local level and they at the republican level. Four, go for a change of policy of with the aim of creating a Greater Serbia."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Shoup, if you'd known about this document --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- would you have written that line?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to comment on that comment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Radovan Neskovic, so I'm sure he would use the term Greater Serbia. I'm sure that Milorad Ekmecic would use the term Greater Serbia. He was known as a die-hard historian, one of the more sinister forces I think in this whole story. And as far as Radovan Neskovic is concerned, I can't say. I don't want to prolong my answer. I could explain that when I said a Greater Serbia, what I meant and repeat that, but perhaps you don't want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying these are the opinions of these individuals. I know Ekmecic. I'm not surprised at all he would take that position using the term Greater Serbia. Radovan Neskovic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, Professor, all I'm asking you is if you had seen this document and others which talk about the Greater Serbia, would you have said in terms that the Serbs never themselves laid out a plan for a Greater Serbia? That's all I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you say "the Serbs," I'm thinking primarily of Belgrade. When I was making my comments yesterday, I was thinking of the famous memorandum of 1986. I would never say that about individuals within any of these groups, especially within Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if you wish to say that within the SDS, somebody was laying out a plan for a Greater Serbia, yes, I'm sure that somebody was. I don't think Milosevic was. And I don't think the Serbian intellectuals of 1986 were. And we'll take it at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Professor, we were talking about it, at least I thought we were, through this whole of your evidence about the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then let me make a further comment. I also said in that testimony that local Serbs even when they might have -- when an individual such as Radovan Neskovic might have spoken about a Greater Serbia were really not interested in the other elements of that Greater Serbia, such as Kosovo. Now, I refer to you Misha Glenny's book in which he is absolutely startled by the fact that the intellectuals in Croatia, the Serbian intellectuals in Croatia couldn't care less about Kosovo, and that was to what I was referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may be confused. Is the Prosecutor suggesting that if one person makes a speech calling for a Greater Serbia that that represents a Serb plan?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't proposing to pull out every single document that refers to a Greater Serbia. I am suggesting, and I have suggested throughout the whole trial from the evidence that there was indeed a plan which was called, putting it in its global thing, a plan for Greater Serbia. And if I haven't made that clear throughout the trial and from the evidence we've called, then I apologise. But at the moment, all that I am asking or was asking Professor Shoup is whether he wouldn't have changed that rather sweeping statement if he'd known about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Now, at page 47 of the same LiveNote, you said this: First, in the report you were asked about -- I should put it in context for you. It was dealing with the Bosnian Assembly in October. And you were read various passages by Mr. Ackerman. And then you were asked this: "It appears almost as if Izetbegovic isn't taking what Karadzic is saying seriously. Why does he respond in such a way that there will be no war?" And you replied, page 47: "First, in the report, I repeat over and over and over again that all sides were preparing for war, even on the Muslim side in self-defense." And then you repeat -- you say that this comment by Izetbegovic is meant to reassure as much as anything the international community, and I'm skipping what you said about this.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you went on to say this: "The reason is very simple. He doesn't want the threat of war or fear of war to in any way pose an obstacle to the recognition of Bosnia, which he, and I understand him perfectly, feels is the only way they will be saved from a war in which they will be the possible losers." Now, that's right, isn't it, Professor? If the Muslims were preparing for war, it's because they realised that the Serbs were preparing for war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. And the Serbs were preparing for war because they realised the Bosnians were preparing for war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry. That's not what you actually said, though. What did you mean by the words, "Even on the Muslim side in self-defense"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I think that all sides considered that what they were doing was self-defense. I don't -- I mean, we can talk about -- they had irreconcilable goals. That's all I can say. And they were going to fight it out. I can't put it any more simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you understand by the words "self-defense"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-defense means that they fear the other side is going to take over their villages, is going to tell them -- and they are going to defend themselves, and that the other side is going to use force to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truth is, isn't it, Professor Shoup, and you effectively, I suggest, admitted it that it was the Serbs who were preparing all out for war, and the Muslims were reacting in self-defense?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fundamentally correct because the Muslims had -- were, after all, still in charge of the central government in Bosnia. And from that point of view, they could wait and see what the Serbs would do, yeah. Mm-hmm, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I just want you to look, then, I was going to show you a number of documents, but I want you to look, please, now at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me just a moment. I just want to check one document first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like you to have a look on this topic, please, at Exhibit P34. While that's being looked for, Professor Shoup, does the document which has been sometimes called the variant A and B document mean anything to you? Instructions for the organisation and activity of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances. Professor? Professor, no, no --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't want me to obviously read this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, just pause. That's not the document I'm showing you. I just want to know if you've ever heard --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I think in Professor Donia's testimony, or I could confuse it with Mr. Brown's testimony, there is reference to the A and B variants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you read that testimony, had you ever heard of it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you yourself has never seen the document?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, you're quite right. I don't require you to read through the whole document. Could you look, please, at page 36 in the translation. This is part of Dr. Karadzic's speech on the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 36 in the translation, Your Honour. At the bottom, page 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic is saying that the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is basically a conflict among peoples, just as it was the case between India and Pakistan, and that's nothing new. It resulted in a huge resettlement of the people.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can interrupt, I want to find where you're quoting him. But never mind, I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the fourth paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Muslims cannot live with others. We must be clear on that. They could not -- they couldn't live with the Hindu, who are as peaceful as sheep. That's the Indian religion. They are a peaceful people, and yet they couldn't live with them. They couldn't live with the Greek on Cyprus. They couldn't live in the Lebanon with Arabs of the same blood, same language, but of a different faith. There can be no discussion here. Yet they set up the Bosnian Krajina there, and in two years' time you would have problems again to separate each and every village there because they will overwhelm you with their birthrate and their tricks. We cannot allow that to happen." Now, were you aware of that speech by Dr. Karadzic before you looked at this document?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you move, please, to the next page. That's page 37, and can you find about halfway down the words indented: "We have to take the status of the Serbs into account."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found that spot, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Please, until two or three months ago, we were hoping to be able to play the Yugoslav card and to save the Yugoslav army, Yugoslavia, legality, et cetera. This is slipping out of our grasp. That is why we started on another track, a Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our sovereign right, our army. We are preparing the constitutional framework to be able to have immediately and on the basis of the negotiations in Lisbon, to have a National Guard, to have our own police force, to have a government to turn the Yugoslav Army into the Army of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, I take it you had -- because you hadn't read this before, you had not heard about Karadzic saying this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although it doesn't seem out of character or unlike things I've seen him say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you, Professor Shoup, that it shows two things: One is a real antipathy, whether for the public or whether he believed it privately, towards the Muslims as a race or as an ethnic person?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, that they were, as it were, negotiating, hoping that they could pretend this was going to be Yugoslav, but having now to accept that this was going to be a Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: There does seem to be a certain way that you're phrasing this. Mr. Karadzic here seems to be very manipulative and cynical in his speech. I believe even in the light of what he -- the tone that he uses, that their desire to be part of Yugoslavia was sincere and genuine and heartfelt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I am suggesting to you is that what he is saying here shows that they were attempting, as it were, to hoodwink the international negotiators or international negotiations by saying this was going to be Yugoslavia, and now they were forced to accept that it wasn't going to be Yugoslavia; it was going to be Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a part of my answer would depend on the date of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's dated February of 1992. The 28th.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: February of 1992. Mm-hmm. All right. We are in a situation where the Badinter commission back on November 29th of the previous year had already said that Yugoslavia was in dissolution. So with that background, I would imagine that they would -- this is entirely in keeping with their strategy, and with the fact that they have been creating institutions even before February 1992 to lay claim to territory in Bosnia. So I don't see that this -- it sounds a little bit more devious when he says this, but I don't see that it reveals anything that we didn't know about the SDS policy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That's all I want you to look at on that document. Could you now look, please, at P50. This is the minutes of the Assembly of the 12th of May 1992. Again, something you've never seen before.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that a very important Assembly was held on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware within the context of a lot of material that was mentioned in, for instance, Professor Donia's accounts of these meetings. Yes, I do remember the 12th of May being mentioned more than once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's not the main point that I want to deal with you on this, but if you go to the very end of the minutes, page 60.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have page 46 as the last page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I've got a -- can I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in Serbo-Croatian. In Cyrillic, it's fine, I can read it. It suggests maybe you have a different version than I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your last page, could you look at that? What's the number that's stamped on the top?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a different version. Because I've got --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the one that ends with 00913562?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've got a copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think what may have happened is we replaced the original minutes with a fuller translation, and obviously it has not gone into the Court file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you look now, please, at page 60, which you have got now --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have page 60. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the draft decision on establishing the Serbian Republic of BH Army --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we see Mr. Krajisnik saying: "Is anyone against -- who's in favour? Is anyone against," that's Momcilo at the bottom: "Abstaining? No one. Serbian gentlemen, I congratulate you on your army." So you see that --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you actually to have a look, please, at page 13.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I'm trying. I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third paragraph: "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presidency, the government, the Council for national security, with which we have set up --" sorry. "Which we have set up have formulated strategic priority. That is to say, the strategic goals for the Serbian People." Now, were you aware of those strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are six of them. I think I may have memorised them. I may not have, but I can tell you generally. If you want me to repeat, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I just want to know when did you first become aware that they had set out these six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reading the materials that were given to me. Again, I think it was Professor Donia's account where they were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before you were shown Professor Donia's account, you had never heard that the Serbs had -- the Bosnian Serbs had set out in their Assembly of the 12th of May the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because of the Graz agreement, we knew pretty much all of those goals. That was made public and is contained in our book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, whatever you know about the Graz agreement, the six strategic goals were not set out in that, were they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Graz agreement? They were all there in one form or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the first such goal is separation from the other two national communities.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Separation of states. Separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state. Now, that, would you accept, Professor Shoup, was effectively the blueprint for what became known as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to think about that. This is certainly a component of ethnic cleansing, not a blueprint, but a component.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And taken with what you saw Karadzic saying in February about the Muslims, it was, was it not, a policy designed to - I'm putting it in the vernacular - get rid of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An articulated policy?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never or you're unaware, are you, of any such expressed goal by Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of such an expressed goal by Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can give that document back to the usher. And finally, I'm just going to, Your Honour, see if there's one more... Yes, could you have finally, on this topic, please, the minutes of the Republika Srpska Assembly, 8th of January 1993, P2449.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you turn to a speech made by Mr. Kupresanin. Do you know who Mr. Kupresanin was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't run across his name frequently in our research, but I assume that it's the same man who appears in Donia's testimony, as I believe the president of the crisis committee at one point in -- am I thinking about the same person? It's not somebody I'm very familiar with. I agree. But I know there was some very, very negative remarks that Donia alluded to, and I think it was he who was making them. Yes, please, which page did you wish me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's at page 64, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kupresanin is effectively going back and having a look at what happened. And can you turn to the bottom of page -- come to the bottom of page 65.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. "We say that this war was not necessary"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's not all together clear here what he means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say because it was -- I've had the translation checked and that's what it does actually say. Or the original checked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was necessary. Right now, if we were to count the population right now, there will be over a million Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina would be predominantly a Serb republic." And then: "Is war necessary in Serbia? It is a horrible thing to say that the war would be necessary in Serbia. If Serbia does not go into the war now, then in three to five years, the Albanians and Muslims will entirely legally overtake the power in Belgrade, along with the Serb opposition. This war was necessary for the Serb people. It is now another question if the Serb people had played the role which had been assigned to them? Gentlemen, you know that we entered the war with the most modern weapons. I am not blaming the generals or the officers. The generals and the Serb Army did not have adequate Serb leaders. Nobody had told these gentlemen, Serb officers, gentlemen, this and that is your task. After all, the Serb Democratic Party was not preparing the Serb people for war. We do remember that our leaders, and I am not criticising here, but only trying to point out the mistakes we made, were told that there will be no war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that we will politically solve the problem. That is exactly what is going on in Geneva, but they have been pulling our leg for years. Now, we go back to this: We had aviation, howitzers, tanks, cannons, but what did Muslims have? Some gun. Some machine-gun that they brought from the Serbs, and homemade guns. We could have gone through Bosnia as through cheese, but have not done it." Now, Professor, one of the things that you talked about was that when you were, as it were, assigning blame to all sides, that the Muslims were armed or were arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did -- sorry. To be correct, I included in the report the extent to which each side was armed as it was set out in the CIA "Balkan Battlegrounds."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's one of the problems, isn't it? I'm going to show you another document, please, on the question of what arms exactly the Muslims did have. Can you have a look, please -- I mean, I'm sorry, before I do that. You see what Kupresanin had to say about the arms that the Serbs had and the arms that the Muslims had?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it's Kupresanin versus the CIA, I guess, at this point, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your point of view, who do you think is likely to be more accurate?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The CIA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to think about that answer for a moment, Professor. Are you seriously saying that the CIA, using open and secondary sources is likely to be more accurate than one of the Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, I didn't concede that the figures the CIA were giving were necessarily based entirely on open sources. I'm not convinced of that. But I do think that they were tasked to do this job and that they did it professionally, whereas Kupresanin is trying to make a point here. He is being a politician. He's saying: "We should have been able to beat up the Muslims. Why didn't we?" This is why he is saying that they don't have any of these weapons because he wants to say: "We should have been more aggressive."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I rather think -- well, what he says -- sorry, going back to it for a moment, is: "We have aviation, howitzers, tanks, cannons." I don't know, Professor, were you aware that witnesses have given evidence of this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that during this trial witnesses have given evidence of the sort of arms that the Serbs actually had?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. I could only provide in my report what seemed to be the best, up-to-date knowledge that we all sure. If the CIA didn't bother to read your reports, they are to blame, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the Muslims have? Some guns, some machine guns that they bought from the Serbs, and homemade guns but have not done it. So he's saying we could have defeated the Muslims, do you accept, but didn't do it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I accept that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that that's what he says. I'm not sure that that's correct or not. I'm really not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think I disagree with him, too, as I think about it because when I think about the whole -- the situation, different parts of Bosnia at that particular moment, in January 1993 when the Muslim forces have reached the Drina River, it's just about now. This takes us back to what we mentioned earlier, and they are shelling the Serbian side. In Cazinska Krajina, around Bihac, the Muslims are holding out perfectly well, thank you. When the Serbs have been forced out of Mostar, well, they will be forced out in a few months from this. And I'm not sure how he can say they can go through Bosnia like cheese. I really don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to this business of the "Balkan Battlegrounds," as you say.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you were read, as I said, page 306, which I think everybody now has copies of, and this is page 69 of the LiveNote for the 5th of February. And one of the things that the report, the CIA report says is that the VRS focussed on seizing weapons from the population. Do you recall that? Have you got page 306?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you distribute the copies of page 306 that you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could he be given the Defence exhibit so that we are referring to a document that's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. This is part of the conclusion that was read to you. And you just said you thought the CIA report was more accurate than what Mr. Kupresanin had to say. Now, I want you to --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they are that different. I don't want to interrupt you. I do apologise to the Court, but I realise that we have to go back. The CIA report was talking mostly about numbers of persons in the various Muslim organisations. And I think we should read what they said about the number of arms to see if there is a contradiction. I'm not sure right now without checking back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you think there is, I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you, Professor Shoup, that the evidence from the documents and from testimony suggests or shows that it wasn't the VRS who were responsible for collecting -- seizing weapons, but the police, the CSB and the SJB?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. I can't possibly contest the evidence as it's given here in the Court. If it's a suggestion that the CIA got it wrong, then I have no difficulty with that except to say that I'm disappointed that this very professional organisation has let us all down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the problem, Professor Shoup, that as I suggest and I thought you'd agreed, that they rely on open-source material. In fact, they say so in their introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the fourth time now that Mr. Shoup has been asked about this. He has said every time that he does not believe they relied on open-source material, that they also relied on material that they had developed in other ways. I don't know how many times he has to say it. But Ms. Korner is now suggesting at line 24 and 25 that she thought he agreed, and he has never agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I think the witness can answer for himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have "Balkan Battlegrounds, Volume I"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have this page 306. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you give your witness a copy of "Balkan Battlegrounds, Volume I." I'm sorry? I thought it was an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, "Balkan Battlegrounds, Volume I" is not an exhibit. I don't have it, I've never had it. You have it. I saw it over on your desk. But I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have been given --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, because you rely on -- you know, Professor Shoup, you rely, do you not, partly, as one of the sources of "Balkan Battlegrounds, Volume I."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do need to clarify that point. I have submitted to the Court in my report the evidence produced by these research organisations. I actually question some of the findings of the CIA in the report itself, as you know I do. Therefore, I'm offering to the Court what the latest, up to date and very professional assessment is, and also pointing out where I have doubts about that. So I don't rely on it in that sense, except in places where they give us data such as the armaments of the two sides and so forth. It seems to me that's the best place to go. But not their conclusions always, no, I don't rely on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right:

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm rather surprised because if -- well, never mind. I'll just get on with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you then what it says at page 16 of the introduction to "Balkan Battlegrounds."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is volume I?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Volume I, Your Honour. It's the only one we could get hold of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Given the dearth of primary archival material, the authors' research for this project relied heavily on local and western daily press accounts by radio, television, and wire services. Contemporary local newspaper or magazine interviews with military commanders, articles in wartime, and post-war official military journals and the memoirs of some of the commanders."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you don't quote everything that they say, which is important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll give you the book, and you can tell me what else you think is important.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may take me a minute to find it, but I'll just summarise what they also say. And that is, we discovered, that is, the CIA team, that we could learn a great deal by cross-checking the information given in the sources that you cite on one side against the same -- against the accounts on the other side, and that they also say that we were surprised the extent to which local newspapers would report on the activities of -- around their front. I'm sure you'll find that if you want to there in that account. I was surprised, too. I thought they wouldn't get much material in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll certainly give you the book because I don't want in any way to mislead the Court on this. And finally, on page 17 of this introduction, "We gratefully acknowledge our debt to BBC Worldwide Limited, Penguin, and to authors Laura Silber and Allan Little for allowing us to quote liberally from their book "Yugoslavia: Death of a Nation" which helped provide much of the political context for our military analysis."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm glad they acknowledged the -- it's an excellent book, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you the book over the break, Professor, and then you can look for any other bits that you want to tell the Court about.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to have a look, please, at P271 on this question of arms and who was doing the disarming. This is a document which, again, I imagine you haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is signed by someone called Stojan Zupljanin. Do you know who Stojan Zupljanin was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what he is talking about in this -- it's actually, I think the date is -- it would appear to be July, I think. Maybe May, because there's a second one attached. Right, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just realised I need to check one of the... Your Honour, I just realised I stapled together two documents which are different exhibits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an order to the public security stations, and it says: "With a view to monitoring the disarmament of paramilitary formations, armed groups and formations in possession of illegal firearms and ammunition in the area of Banja Luka CSB and with a view of following the outcome of this operation, all SJBs are obliged to submit to the centre detailed information on these disarmament operations up to and inclusive of the 15th of June 1992." And then it lists the information which is required, weapons and ammunition returned voluntarily in response to the order issued by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and various descriptions. Now, the next document, and I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's not on my list because I clipped the two together by mistake. We're just checking what the number is and we'll get it out ourselves. It's P1288. And we'll just -- we'll put it up on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For some reason, I don't believe they brought the exhibits to the Court today. So we'll have to hand it out ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid you'll have to look at it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I clipped the two together without realising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the response to the request or order from Stojan Zupljanin from Prijedor, dated the 5th of July. You can see that it's a response because it says: "Reference your dispatch number 11-1/04." It was the 1st of July, that date. "In reference to your dispatch with the above number and date, please note the following: In keeping with the order of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, 2 M-48 rifles, 2 automatic rifles, and 4 pistols and 55 bullets have been returned." There is then a description, Serb description of the fighting in Hambarine and Kozarac. "Four, most weapons and ammunition were seized in the fighting in Hambarine and Kozarac. Some seized weapons are currently in the possession of military organs. Most of the weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence of Hambarine and Kozarac were returned to the army. There is some information that the arm and the police seized weapons and kept them for themselves or gave them to others to use. Our station's records regarding seized and collected weapons and ammunition as follows: 16 automatic rifles, 7 M-48s, 184 hunting rifles, 24 hunting carbines, 8 MK rifles, 445 pistols -- .9 millimetre pistols, 280 7.65 millimetre, 90 7.62 calibre pistols, 6.35 calibre pistols, pistol ammunition and hunting ammunition."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you agree, Professor Shoup - and this is the Prijedor record - that the Muslim side were hardly armed to the same extent as the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you to the extent that this document does not prove that. I believe you're correct, but I don't believe it on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you suggest to the witness what, according to the records that we have, was the population of Muslims in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not without checking, Your Honour, no. I could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, that may be relevant for his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to explain why I don't believe it on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime, go ahead, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll tell you why. Because these people -- I believe that this was, generally speaking, the situation. I don't think the people in this region were terribly heavily armed, but I also know from experience this whole Balkan practice, that when you think a war is about to break out, you bury your arms. You do not make it easy to find. And later you then dig them up and go to war. So I suspect in a city such as Prijedor this probably wasn't happening, but the number of arms they find is no indication of how many arms the Muslims may have had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know, do you know anything about the attacks on Kozarac and Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. That is, the details. I know that they took place, but not the details. I agree with your general conclusion so that we are not in disagreement with each other. I'm simply saying that this document doesn't prove your contention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the wrong volume. Volume I. Your Honour, in fact, this will do, Your Honour. It's not the census document, but it's a rough... This is -- Your Honour, this is not the census document we've all looked at. It's Exhibit 1150, which shows that Prijedor contained 112.470 inhabitants of which 49.454 were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So roughly plus or minus 50.000 Muslims in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There were also 6.300 Croats and 47.745 Serbs. Your Honour, this is the 23rd of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think, Professor Shoup, if I'm wrong, you are, in fact, agreeing with me that the Muslims had nothing like the weaponry that was available to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, especially if we're talking about Bosanska Krajina. This particular region. I think we should go region by region. But I certainly -- in the context of this region around Prijedor and Banja Luka, I would certainly agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one of the other things that you said, again on the 5th of February, and this is the LiveNote at page 92, is -- and this was in answer to questions by me, the very beginning of cross-examination when I asked you whether you were trying to -- you were not trying to suggest, are you, that because Bosnia was dysfunctional that excuses the commission of war crimes by individuals, and you said: "I'm trying to suggest that war crimes must sifted through, a Balkan situation, and not for us to stand off and try to apply standards and imagine the Bosnian situation as one that we're more comfortable with. That is, one that is not as complicated and so on. I think that's what was done during the war itself. We had to talk about a war of aggression because we felt more comfortable with it." Now, in the light of what we have been looking at today and Friday, it was a war of aggression, wasn't it, that the Serbs were waging?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The background of the Serb actions, as you know, is a total incompatibility between Bosnian Muslim aims for the Republic of Bosnia with the aims of the Serbs. Both of them are using nationalistic language which I really find very repellent, frankly. They were both preparing for war against one another. I've said time and time again that the situation really was leading to war. I believe that both sides felt that by early 1992. And it was not a question of aggression by Serbia, as I see it. They had incompatible aims. They wanted to secede. Izetbegovic said you could not secede. And they decided to go to war to secede. Yes, in that sense, if you recognise that Bosnia was a state and people were rebelling against the state. But I have said over and over in my testimony that I don't think Bosnia any longer existed. It was a dysfunctional state. Just like Badinter had said of Yugoslavia, it had ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accepting for the moment what you say, that Bosnia -- and this is purely for the purposes of this argument -- but that Bosnia didn't exist and it was a dysfunctional state. It was still, was it not, a war of aggression by the Serbs on the Muslims by and large?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, I guess I would have to say the Muslims were carrying out a war of aggression against the Serbs in areas where similar actions were taking place around Sarajevo, where the Serbs were placed in camps and so forth and dislocated. May I just close my remarks, I'm not out of sympathy with your position. The Serbs were using their arms. They were in a much stronger position, and they were going to take advantage of that situation. Looked at from the point of view of the local situation, I would be glad to agree with you. But not in Bosnia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I'm sorry. I thought we dealt with this. Some half hour ago or so, you agreed that what you had said yourself was that the Muslims were acting in self-defense.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everywhere. Well, everybody was. Everybody was both aggressing [sic] against the other side and acting in self-defence. My point which I'm trying to get across if you look at all of Bosnia, you will see that people were doing the same thing everywhere. If you want to label it as aggression in Bosanska Krajina against the Muslims, then I suggest you label it as aggression against the Serbs in Konjic, for example, by the Muslims. So everybody is committing aggression against everyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that's what you would like to say, but Professor Shoup in actual reality, and it's not my position, it's what I'm suggesting to you, the evidence clearly shows is that the aggressors were the Serbs, for one very simple reason if nothing else, that the Muslims had no arms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I agree with you when it comes to Prijedor and Banja Luka. I don't agree with you when it comes to Bosnia as a whole. Let's take the situation in Mostar or on the Neretva River. The Croatians and Muslims joined forces in 1992. They expelled the Serbs from Mostar, as you know. Now, are they committing aggression against the Serbs in Mostar? I can't ask you a question, but it would be the one that I would ask you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right, Professor, I don't think that I'm going to continue this argument. You accept, do you, that in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, from what you know about it, which isn't --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we want to use the term "aggression" in this fight hat was going on, I think it's inappropriate since everybody is committing aggression against everybody else but if it suits you best, I will certainly say, all right, here's where the Serbs are predominant, let's use the word "aggression.".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, Professor, I don't want you to say: "What suits you best." I am asking you if alone some of the documents I have shown you this morning and some from what you know of your own knowledge don't reveal clearly that the Serbs were the -- the Bosnian Serbs were the aggressor in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of documents you will show me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of documents you have seen yourself.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I repeat what I said before. The war was going in one direction in the south. It was going in another direction in the north. A third direction in the east. And you're saying that the people who are winning are the aggressors. Well, if that's your standard then I would say that the Muslims and the Croats are aggressors in Mostar and the Serbs are aggressors in Banja Luka, simply because that happens to be the side that is winning of in any given area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to go back and ask you then what you meant when you said yourself in answer to Mr. Ackerman that the Muslims were -- I'm sorry, I better find the part again and read you back what you said. Page 47, LiveNote: "I repeat over and over and over again that all sides were preparing for war even on the Muslim side in self-defense."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, preparing for war means you have to prepare for the defence of your own ethnic bastions; for example, Sarajevo in the case of the Muslims, maybe Banja Luka or Pale in the case of the Serbs. I don't know what else to say here. In a war, there is defence, offence, but certainly -- I don't see the tactics being much different except that the Serbs had the stronger -- were the stronger side in most parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You say: "Even on the Muslim side in self-defense." I asked you about this earlier this morning --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everybody --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That the Muslims were preparing for war to defend themselves, to protect themselves. What else does an ordinary English word like that mean?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that a war is looming. It means that the Serbs have the overwhelming military advantage prior to the war. So it's quite -- that the Muslims are anticipating that the Serbs will attack the Muslims. That is what happened. It's also what happened is that the Muslims allied themselves with the Croatians in the south and took the attack to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you said something, and it hasn't come out on the screen, about the Muslims preparing for the attack.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's not your fault, Professor Shoup. It's the transcript that won't cover the entirety of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could that be marked, it's at line 18, page 41, so when the tape is listened to, it can be corrected. Your Honour, that's probably an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to leave that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to leave that particular discussion, Professor Shoup, which doesn't seem to me to be getting very productive. Could you have your report back again, please. And could you turn to page 18.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, you're talking about first of all the memorandum of sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're aware, aren't you, that Amendment 60 of the 1990 amendments to the Bosnian constitution declared Bosnia a sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, and I'll show it to you if you want -- are you aware, are you not, that in --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amendment 60 of the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amendment 60 --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adopted in 1990, I presume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
