utterances.text: That's right. Declared that the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a democratic sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those declarations of sovereignty were common in the republics at that time. They weren't obviously taken to mean at that moment in 1990 that Bosnia-Herzegovina was declaring its independence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. No, I just wanted to -- because it wasn't the first time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the first time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to deal with the debate over the plans to hold a referendum. You don't mention there the plebiscite that was held in November 1991. But you're aware of it, I know.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. As you can see, I'm trying to summarise what was already submitted into evidence, that is, the book, and not to go into excruciating detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then in the third paragraph, do you see the sentence: "By this time, the Serbs had already formed SAOs."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the third paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "That seemed bent on secession."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed as you rightly say in your book at page 73, you deal with this in much more detail.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's the chapter, the dissent into war, page 73: "Serb autonomous oblast were formed in Serb areas of Bosnia, the SAO in eastern and old Herzegovina was established on September the 12th."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The SAO of Bosanska Krajina on --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- September 16th." And so on. "This continued the process of wresting control away from Sarajevo started by the Serbs in October 1990." All right, now, then could you move, please, to the next -- I'm sorry, page 20 where you summarise the factors at work which made --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A constitutional agreement in Bosnia so difficult.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the second factor that you summarise: "Were the actions of the Serb and Croat break away regions in declaring autonomy on the one hand and the Bosnian Assembly in declaring sovereignty and pushing independence on the other."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We are not able to say at this point which action provoked the other."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the declaration of the SAOs was in September of 1991. The declaration of sovereignty, pushing for independence, was in October 1991. So how do you say you're not able to say which action provoked the other?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure, as the Prosecution is aware, that the motion to declare Bosnia sovereign, which is in this case and in this context a very serious move, we agree, that that motion was made twice earlier and not accepted in the spring of -- this would be the spring of 1991, before the SAOs were formed. And that's why I'm not going to prejudge the issue of who started all of this. Frankly, I think they were both intent on their own agendas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But -- so when you said the break away regions in declaring autonomy and the Bosnian Assembly and declaring sovereignty and pushing for independence, you didn't mean the actions of September 1991 but you meant something earlier? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that in mind. As I said, I don't try in this report to go into great detail. But what is influencing my statement here is the fact that at least -- well, not at least but two efforts were made prior to October 15th in the Bosnian Assembly to declare sovereignty for reasons that are not clear to me, they were not -- the resolutions were not adopted. I think that was as early as January or February of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we should read into your sentence there: "Earlier attempts."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm. Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say this: "It was clear, to be fair to the Muslim side --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "-- that once the formation of the AOs was underway, the SDA could rightly feel that any compromise in the direction of regionalisation of Bosnia would in the end lead to Bosnia's dismemberment." Why did you need to adds add the words: "To be fair to the Muslim side." Aren't you trying to be fair to all sides?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- the declaration -- by focussing on the adoption of the declaration of sovereignty without the approval of the Serbs on October 15th, we see what is a really very basic violation of the rights of one of the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I felt it was not fair to leave it at that, that we had to point out the dilemma in which the Bosnian Muslim side faced, and that was that given the fact that these SAOs were now in existence, any compromise in the direction of regionalisation of Bosnia could lead to the -- could simply lead to the further dismemberment of Bosnia. This is a terrible dilemma for all sides, it seems to me. I don't think anyone would say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's not, is it, that your report starts from - putting it in as neutral a term as I can find - a predisposition to look at the point of view of the Serbs throughout?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I may inadvertently give that impression. I certainly -- and this is precisely why this sentence is here, to show the dilemma in which the Muslims were at this point. I don't want to look at it only from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to deal very briefly, then, please with something you say in your report on the military side. Page 27. Now, you talk about there in paragraph 3: "On the other hand, the war was not all as one-sided as observers initially thought."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Croat forces with Bosnian Muslims in their ranks drove the Serbs from Mostar. The struggle over establishing a corridor between Western Bosnia and Semberija first ended in defeat for the Serbs, and the fight for the corridor continued throughout the war."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again I ask you how much detail do you know about the fight for the corridor?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not examined the war in Bosnia from a strictly military viewpoint. However, I was -- I've spent many hours trying to determine just generally what did happen in those months after April of 1992. As I -- I don't know that if I have to recapitulate this, but I will be brief, and that is that initially there was an offensive from the north by the Muslims and the Croatians. It was the Croatians who were the chief instigators of this invasion. They pushed south. This would be -- I won't maybe get the dates exactly right. This would have to be June of 1992. Then the Serbs -- and that, of course, broke the corridor, at least for a week or two. And then the -- or more. And then the Serbs counterattacked and, as we know, opened the corridor again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. This is what you say. You said that it ended in defeat for the Serbs, and the fight for the corridor continued throughout the war. But that's, may I suggest, an inaccurate statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the first offensive that was launched in the corridor was launched by the Croatians and the Muslims and led to defeat by the Serbs, as I just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you base this on? Military documents?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness. That was -- I have gone over that, you know -- I couldn't possibly tell you, on the -- if the question is, did that happen or not, I would stand firmly on the position yes, exactly that's what happened. That was way back ten years ago that that material was first, you know, looked at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You see, I'm going to suggest to you that the evidence from the Serbs own military documents shows that the corridor was cut, as you say rightly, by the Croat and Muslim forces. It was then retaken, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And thereafter-wards was expanded by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. That's basically what I said a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the fight to the corridor continued, the corridor thereafter was open?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the fight to widen it continued. The forces were entrenched on each side, but the fighting continued along the corridor. I will simply mention, because it's fresh in my mind, the CIA reports make a big point of the fact that a great number of Serb forces were tied down on the corridor and could not be used elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you look, please, next at page -- just for a moment, to page 28. Just one thing I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in the third paragraph: "While we tend to think of the conflict as one of irregular forces." Who's "we"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the editorial "we".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but I am -- here, there is a tendency to be a little, let's say, flexible. When I say: "When we tend to think," I mean that not only I, but that was the general impression at the time the war was being fought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- well, that's what I'm getting at. Who do you say had this impression apart from you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't cite the -- the articles are in the book. But there were articles that were appearing frequently in military journals such as Jane's Intelligence, I forget the exact title of that magazine, painting this war in very picturesque terms. For example, I can cite one article, I could find it for you here, which described how one side that was on the higher side of the hill would pack dynamite in a rubber tube and roll it down the hill on the other side. This seemed to be like a primitive way of fighting wars, and you had other examples of this kind which gave that impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I lost -- just trying to find a note that I made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I was going to deal with something, but I can't now find the note I was looking for. Your Honour, I'll move on, and I may come back to that later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you look, please, next at page 33.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sorry. Page 41.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 41?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is where you are talking about effectively your thesis of the demonisation of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't use that term here, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you use it earlier on, but that's what you're talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the fact that acts which --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. Sorry, stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go back to the top of page 41, the first paragraph: "To be clear, there was reason to be outraged by the Serb atrocities committed against the Muslims but this observer in any case became deeply troubled by --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, I do use the term. If I might explain, it's simply that what follows is an explanation of why no one believed that the Muslims might have shelled their own people. But...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the -- is your thesis or whatever you want to call it, demonisation, is that based entirely on this incident in the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely not. No. It's based --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You keep on going back to it, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shows you how far it went. That is, nobody would believe that the Muslims might have done this when the facts indicate that we don't know and that the Muslims were also capable of shelling their own people. It shows you how far this whole tendency to blame the Serbs for everything went, and this is in the -- I think this is a very important point to make in front of the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we look at the third of your conclusions: "The outrage over these incidents and the rush to blame one side reflected the fact that the Serbs often refused to cooperate with international observers in Bosnia. Out of suspicion of the IC's motives..." That's the international community, I take it: "...and persuaded that the media would use any opportunity given them to engage in Serb bashing," as you so put it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at another document, 2425. Now this, again, is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 3rd of September, which, again, I take it, you've never looked at?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the 3rd of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And it's headed state of morale in the 1st Krajina Corps units --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- In August of 1992. If you go, please, to the second page of the translation.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "All units and armed formations have essentially been put under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although there is still resistance from the CSB.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm suggesting certainly by August 1992 the so-called paramilitary formations were actually under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on the point that you make at the bottom of that page: "The effect of combat morale of the resolution of the Serbian Republic crisis by the international community, the intolerant attitude of the international community towards the Serbs' position in BH is causing extreme distrust of their goodwill. In this period, there was great interest in visits to LRZs," which I think is camps, "...with euphoria the dominant feeling, interest in the sick and difficult cases and the attempts to show the world public the unbearable conditions in these camps."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then deal with the visit by Mr. Mazowietski to what was Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then can you go down to the next part: "The effect of the political security situation in the territory --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please could the counsel slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Certain tensions --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect of the political and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ... present in the Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor areas.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat that. Now I've lost you. Last paragraph: "Certain tensions were still present." Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to start again because I see, and it's my fault, I'm sorry, I'm going too fast. The transcript hasn't picked up the beginning. "Certain tensions are still present in the Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor areas because of a large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The CSB especially from Prijedor is not contributing to this approach. Prijedor, headed by --" that should be Simo, it's Stevo Drljaca, "...who led a convoy of people who wanted to leave the crisis area. They committed a massacre in the Skender Vakuf area of over 150 men who wanted to leave the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "This action caused indignation, not only among citizens, but also among 1st Krajina Corps soldiers. This dark stain which was created did not have support, but it is very fortunate that the international community did not find out about it in more detail."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Shoup --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shoup, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shoup, I'm sorry. The Serbs themselves were trying to hide things from the international community, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say they were, and I think everybody was. Could I elaborate? I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My experience in doing research is this, and this was what I was trying to say under part 3 on page 41, the Serbs did not really provide the international community with information on what was happening to the Serbs themselves in Bosnia. I found it extremely difficult to find this out. I did, I think, satisfactorily. And this struck me as very odd, and perhaps as a result of the suspicion of the international community, and of me, by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Couldn't it just be that they weren't providing information because they didn't want the international community to know what they were doing? Isn't that an alternative thesis?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these are -- I don't understand -- I know they are hiding what they are doing. You and I are in agreement on that, but I don't know why they would hide what the Muslims were doing to the Serb side, or the Croatians -- not hide it, but make it difficult to find out. This was what I was -- this was my experience and something that puzzled me continually in my research.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, that's the next topic that I want to come on to, Professor, and that's this: That what they were showing to the international community, amongst others, was propaganda suggesting atrocities committed by the other side.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe so, but they didn't make the chapter and verse, that is, the details of those atrocities, easily available. Now, let me qualify that. There were documents sent to the United Nations listing the atrocities that were committed against the Serbs. But to really get a realistic picture of what was happening in Sarajevo in the private prisons, for example, where Serbs were being held and later were exhumed when the war ended, you had to go outside the regular propaganda channels to find this material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to have a look at a video of some of the television programmes that were going out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is actually a brand-new video, which has just come into our possession. And I'm not going to play all of it. But that's going to -- that's happening, and we've done a transcript of some parts and summaries of the others. I'm not going to play the whole thing. Can I hand out the transcripts that we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has it been disclosed to Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2727 it is, Your Honour. So it will be 2727 for the video, 2727.1 for the transcript. We will replace it with a full one, Your Honour, when it's finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Madam Registrar, just make sure that we haven't had 2727 before. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to skip -- there's quite a lengthy part which is -- if Your Honour goes to the transcript at 4.12, it's the third page, there's a piece on Ostojic. It's a reporter talking. We haven't had that transcribed. I'm going to skip from where it goes 4.10 to 08 on the timer. I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The sound does get better, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going to skip.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is just the end of...
