utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the interpreters have got the -- yes, they have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they have, yeah. There is one -- okay, all right. So when we start --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the interpreters know where it starts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where we just started, with the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That isn't Ostojic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't find it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the piece on Ostojic, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which is the page, please, for the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to go back a bit, rewind just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't propose to play any more of the video firstly because we haven't had a chance to properly go through it, translate it, and secondly because it is apparently from the summary it deals with the late of 1993 -- with the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Shoup, having watched that -- now, first of all, were you aware of what that first camp was that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manjaca he's talking about. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard about Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is being alleged in this part of the film from the people that you see is that Manjaca is a camp where conditions are relatively good, where they get medical treatment and the like. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I think it's -- I'm not sure the Prosecutor might wish to amplify this point. As I see it, some of these prisoners are wearing Chetnik hats; is that correct? Which they are probably being forced to wear, to humiliate them. That is my conclusion right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the point of view of conditions what is being suggested by this footage, isn't it, that there was medical treatment, that the food was cooked by a number of professional cooks and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't believe that. And the minute I saw the "sajkaca" on these Muslims' heads, I wouldn't believe a word that they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You might not because, Professor Shoup, you obviously have expertise in this area of the world. What about the ordinary member of the public? And you saw there was an English reporter there, or somebody speaking in English. What would they think?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You're better qualified to say that, except that it's so common for people being held in prisons to say that everything is just fine, that I must say that even an ordinary, intelligent spectator must have had some skepticism about this. But that's just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it then goes on to say, as we all saw, that whilst these people were being looked after in this camp, there were -- sorry, while the Serbs were taking care of their prisoners, fresh graves of known and mass graves of unknown Serbian heroes are spreading all over the Krajina. And then you see those utterly repellent photographs.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so much of that was going that it was terrible. And of course the Serbs were defeating their own cause. Then no one would believe -- when some atrocity was committed against the Serb, nobody would believe it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the Serbs weren't waging a propaganda battle. They were, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said that I had difficulty in getting solid information from the Serbs of what was being done to their own people in areas that were occupied by the Croatians and Muslims. We take it for granted that that means that none of us are looking at the propaganda films for evidence; we are looking for interviews with refugees, we're looking for documentation of the kind that might be submitted to the United Nations, something more serious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, look at page 42 of your report again, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Be this as it may, the Serbs, unlike the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats, did not wage a propaganda battle."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should have added to that "with the international community." Because though propaganda films that we saw are simply not credible, and the Serbs must have known that. Let's take the United Nations. There was a Serb representative at the United Nations during the war. They never effectively took the evidence of what was happening to Serbs in Sarajevo and made a convincing case that something should be done about it. This is perhaps where I should have said: "Didn't wage a propaganda battle where it counted, in the United Nations and elsewhere".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you should have said was, wasn't it, they were pretty hopeless and ineffective at the sort of propaganda they tried to put out?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the international community. Is that what you mean? Well, in general -- I would say in general, yes, I agree with you in general. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the final matter I want to deal with you, and it's on the same topic. And it's what you have to say about the ITN report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the statement, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about what you say about the original ITN report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: ITN. Yes, certainly the incident at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Have you yourself ever seen the news broadcast?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the tape that -- what is it, The Emperor's Clothes, I refer to it here, and point out how they themselves don't tell the whole story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute. You watched The Emperor's Clothes which purported to show that the footage was faked. Why didn't you watch the original?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I think that you're asking me on every single incident that arises to go back and check everything. I thought, and maybe the Prosecutor can straighten me out, that there wasn't any argument about that particular event; that is, that these people were being filmed from -- the prisoners were on the outside, you know, the contention there that the prisoners were on the outside of this barbed wire, and that the film producers were on the inside. And this then went to Court, as we know, in Great Britain. I know that the Court then decided that these people were not considered to have somehow -- what was the word? What would the word be? That they were found not guilty --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Faked the footage.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Faked the footage. That's what the allegation was in this film --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that you knew at the time that you wrote this report that in 2002 - I could have the date wrong - this whole issue had been thrashed out in the libel courts?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that it had been shown to the satisfaction of a jury that this was genuine footage?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the interpretation of the footage that -- could I explain a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue was that the press -- as I say it here, the issue was that the -- that I wanted to stress was that the press took this whole footage up to mean that this was a concentration camp, Trnopolje, and that this was part of what Roy Gutman and the others said, these were deaths camps and so on and so forth. I don't believe -- I'd have to check once more. I don't want to imply that I knew whether the barbed wire was on one side or the other. What we do know is that it was considered to be a concentration camp. And then Penny, whatever her name is, it turns out, never said that. And this was what the film The Emperor's Clothes did not adequately explain. The issue for me was, were people claiming this was a concentration camp or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you what you said -- you have a look at what you said. And I'm going to show you the film that you've never seen, plus some of the testimony about it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent. I'd love to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 42, at the top: "The negative image which the Serbs acquired was in part the result of well-known media dispatches, for example, of death camps by Roy Gutman."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Which circulated in the summer of 1992 and the notorious picture --"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause, would you please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "And the notorious picture of a starved Muslim behind barbed wire taken by an ITN television crew shortly after Gutman's reports began to appear."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "(The individual in question was, in fact, outside the barbed wire, and the location was not a concentration camp, but a relocation centre.)"

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asserted, as a fact, that the individual was outside --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though you were aware that there had been a libel action where the allegation had been dealt with in full and a jury had decided that this film was a genuine film.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that the accusation had been made that this was a concentration camp and that when the issue came in front of the Court, it was shown that Penny, what -- her name, actually made clear that this was not a concentration camp. I was not aware that the Court in any way decided that this film was taken from the outside or the inside. I needed a clarification. Is it true, then, that the Court decided that the film was taken from outside to the inside of the camp? If that was the case, then I have been misled. But I don't know -- but I haven't received the answer, so I don't know otherwise. But my focus was I had assumed that the Court had decided that Penny whatever-her-name-was was not guilty of libel because she didn't say it was a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why before you made this statement, and it takes up a substantial part of this page, why didn't you check?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the material that I read about the decision of the Court, there was no mention of the fact that the film was, in fact, -- you say genuine, but that's ambiguous, that is, that the film was actually taken from the outside looking in. If I had some suspicion of that in the material I had read, I would have certainly gone further. But I had no suspicion that the Court was telling me that the way this was filmed was quite different than what I had thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the issue, not whether Trnopolje was a concentration camp, but whether the two journalists from ITN, Penny Marshall and Iain Williams, had deliberately filmed the inmates outside the wire as though they were inside the wire. That was the whole issue. Didn't you appreciate that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from what you can see in the general discussions of this incident. Now, I'm still not clear whether the decision of the court was that, in fact, they were viewing from the outside into the inside?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor, I suggest that you go and check that yourself. I'm now going to show you the actual film, and then I'm going to show you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've attached to it, Your Honour, part of the testimony from the Stakic case which was an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. I was fooled if that's the case. Let's go.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the film that we have seen --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's P1133, but we've added on to that the actual video of Dr. Merdzanic testifying in Stakic, which is P1148, because it's easier to do it rather than reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, how is this admissible, this testimony from some other case? How can I cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's an exhibit. You can cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't give evidence in this case. He did?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know it has been a long case, Mr. Ackerman. But he gave evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this his testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not his testimony in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is his testimony in Stakic, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's his testimony in Stakic, which is an exhibit because I couldn't go through the whole thing because we have an agreement that the Prijedor witnesses, the testimony of the transcript from Stakic would go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why not use his testimony in this case, then, that has been cross-examined properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- Your Honour, may I explain. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we having the discussion -- are we having this discussion --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, this doesn't affect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to ask the witness go out of the room for a moment because I do have something that I would want to say outside his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Usher. Thank you. And I think with your consensus, Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, thrash this point out, and we can have the break immediately after rather than bring him in and break --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's a very, very long time, and Mr. Ackerman has forgotten. Your Honour, in respect of Prijedor because nearly all the witnesses had testified either in the Stakic case or other cases, the agreement was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Listen --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was standing up so I could get a better look at the picture. I'm sorry, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The agreement was that the transcript of the previous evidence would go in as an exhibit. That was part of their evidence. And then if any additional questions should be asked, then they could be asked. Dr. Merdzanic gave full testimony in Stakic which he didn't give here, but his testimony in Stakic was an exhibit, and is there intended, and I hope that Your Honours have taken it that way, to be evidence to be used in this trial. And anything that was said in the Stakic trial or any of the other trials, if it wasn't accepted by the Defence, had to be cross-examined. Now, I didn't take Dr. Merdzanic through what he had to say about the wire in this trial in his evidence because it was contained in the part of the Stakic transcript. And that's what I'm showing because it's easier and more effective to show the video, so it's the video of his evidence and the exhibit number is 1148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept all of that. I think Ms. Korner is absolutely correct about that, so I have no further objection regarding this particular part here. The other part that I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- I'm a bit concerned about is I thought that the issue of Penny Marshall's television show from Trnopolje was a resolved issue. It's clear that she went inside a barbed wire enclosure for the purpose of filming from that enclosure out of that enclosure into Trnopolje. I mean, you can go there and see it yourself. I have been there many times and seen it myself. If you look at the tape, there's a little short fence about this high that's on the road side that goes in front of Trnopolje school that is a temporary enclosure that was put there. But the actual footage itself, it's still there, there's an enclosure there that has a gas company or something in it that's surrounded by barbed wire. She went inside that enclosure to take the pictures to make it look like this was a camp surrounded by barbed wire. It was not. So I don't know why this is an issue any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just as well Mr. Ackerman has some kind of privilege for saying these things in Court. Because otherwise, I think he'd find himself facing a libel action. It's the exact opposite. That was what the whole libel action was about Mr. Deichman, whoever he might be, alleged that exactly what Mr. Ackerman has now alleged happened, that they went inside the wire, that the prisoners were actually free to wander about, and the whole thing was faked. That is what the whole point was. These prisoners, and that's what Merdzanic said, and that was not cross-examined to, the wire wasn't there for very long, but it was put up over the chicken wire that one can see, and it surrounded three sides of the camp. Penny Marshall, and it's quite clear, stood outside the wire. These prisoners were prisoners inside the camp. And that is exactly what was thrashed out in the libel case. That is what Professor Shoup alleges in this report, without having checked. And clearly it now shows that Mr. Ackerman hasn't checked either. But that is what this was all about. These people were behind the wire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree that -- yes, is there anything else, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've checked and I'm quite certain that I'm right. I have never taken the position that there wasn't a fence. There was a fence. But the barbed wire fence that Penny Marshall takes a picture of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did try to get some witnesses that we have had here agree that there was no fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did try to get some witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, here was a long period of time there was no fence. When they brought the people in -- it's in the transcript, Your Honour, and we probably shouldn't be arguing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite remember what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When they brought people in, they put that fence up temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [previous translation continues]... to the gun posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agree. Your Honour, the evidence is quite clear. Mr. Ackerman is right on that. No wire except for this chicken wire. There were gun posts and sniper posts and everything else. And then when they brought the prisoners over from Omarska and just before that, they put the wire up. That's the evidence. But what we're dealing with here now is the assertion made by Professor Shoup based on this -- it's actually the programme, I think it was untitled, but it was made by a company called The Emperor's Clothes, which repeated Mr. Deichman's libel that Penny Marshall and her crew had stood behind the fence to film the people outside it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Should we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is my last part, so we will finish immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Unless, you want to -- we bring the witness -- how long --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's about -- I think there's about 10 minutes or so of his testimony. So, Your Honour, it may be as well to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I would imagine there is some re-examination, and we may also have some questions for the witness. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've sorted out. Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, because on channel 4 now I'm receiving interpretation in French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've given Mr. Ackerman a copy, and I'm going to be showing it to the witness when the video is finished playing. Can I show you two reports of the libel trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These were not exhibited before, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are not. Your Honour, it has never so far been an issue in this case. It's amazing what has become an issue. If we can have the witness back and finish playing the video, and then I'll ask him a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, where is the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we proceed first, and then I'll give you the opportunity afterwards, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now we are going to refer to the testimony given in the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also in this case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's just the video of what he actually said in Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was page 7751 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was transcript pages 7792 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that last part was transcript page 7795 to 6. Your Honour, because it's a compilation actually of video, could it be given a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand Professor Shoup wanted to say something. He sent you a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Shoup, you asked us to give you an opportunity to respond to the allegation that you perceived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of poor research technique in respect of the Trnopolje incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'll be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I think this particular incident shows the problems of doing research where one might make a mistake, but also where one probably is doing it the right way. I appreciate that I now saw that original film. Having seen that original film of BBC, the critical point where I may have misled the Court about this question of, are people inside the barbed wire or outside the barbed wire I have concluded it could not be determined from that film. Therefore, the research technique that I used which was to consult sources that I trusted that talked about this incident, and I'm referring again to the Dutch study, and never indicated that there was a -- someone alleging that that incident, people inside or outside the barbed wire, was one that had to be looked into. The only way that I would have been able to determine who was right in this case would have probably been to read a secondary source, one that I trusted, which would give a very careful analysis of this situation. I did not find such a source. And finally, let me simply say that there is a tremendous -- a great deal of irony here because I note in the footnote that in fact prisoners had been transferred to Trnopolje from the worst -- the other camps which were worse. And so I was aware of that fact because of the sources I used. I'm aware, therefore, that many of these prisoners who looked maltreated really were maltreated. They had just come from a very much worse camp so that although Trnopolje was not as bad as these other places, prisoners were there who had been very poorly treated, and I think this is all pointed out in the report. What I don't know yet, and maybe the Court can ask the Prosecutor directly, is was the film itself taken of these people with this barbed wire, was it one way or was the other? I will accept the findings of the Prosecutor who has obviously had a chance to look at evidence I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup, we're getting right off the point. The point that I'm trying to make is that you asserted without doing any proper checks at all that this individual, as you put it, was in fact outside the barbed wire. You could have, couldn't you, have done a simple thing like checking on the news reports of the ending of the libel trial.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I relied on the Dutch study, for example, to -- there was no indication there that this allegation had been challenged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, no. The -- well, there are two things. Each time you say something you send me off -- if you would like to have a look, please, at a copy of the Guardian report and the BBC report of the end of the libel trial in 2000.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that, then, become 2729.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both of them together?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all you had to do was look down, wasn't it, and see that the trial and the whole issue concerned what had been called the allegation they deliberately misrepresented the image of an emaciated Bosnian Muslim as being caged behind barbed wire at Trnopolje camp by selective use of camera angles and editing. That's all you had to do, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to read this very carefully before I could answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: So far, I've seen nothing in this report about the -- whether these people were inside or outside the wire. But if I keep reading, maybe I will find out that they were -- they say here that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to delay the Court, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Shoup --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Show me where perhaps because then I can concede the point. Obviously you're better informed than I am. But why don't you show me exactly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will if you stop talking, Professor Shoup, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, of course. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turn to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And go to -- for the Guardian trial [sic], and go to the sixth paragraph, LM's editor.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: LM's editor. "The article claimed the barbed wire was not around the camp which... around the news team, filming from a small enclosure next to the camp." Yes, but I don't have an answer to this paragraph. I mean, I'm willing to concede that this was your point, but I don't see an answer, a straightforward answer to the question of whether these people were filmed inside or outside that particular piece of barbed wire. I'm not trying to defend anybody. I just don't see an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article claimed the barbed wire was not around the camp, but around the news team. Well, we have heard from the testimony here that there was not -- there was a fence around the camp, and I could imagine it was barbed wire, but there wasn't apparently, but there was a fence around the news team: "Filming from a small enclosure next to the camp." Now, I'm looking for someone to say no, that wasn't the way it was. We just -- the next paragraph goes on to claim that the article was an attack on their reputation and professional integrity, and that's all I see. I don't see a refutation of that particular statement. But I'm -- you know, I don't really want to argue, but I would love to know whether that particular incident with the man shown with the barbed wire, whether he was inside or outside the barbed wire. I just don't see it here. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you don't see that in the article?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to waste any more time on it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And in this war, I can concede that what you're saying is quite possible. But apparently, those who did read this article, the Dutch have read everything, plus everything that I never knew they could get to, and didn't reach the same conclusion. There was no clue in these reliable sources that I used that this was an issue, of the barbed wire, and I don't see anything here that suggests otherwise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Dutch report merely reported the controversy. They didn't come down on either side. You relied on, didn't you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just please, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was my turn, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You relied on what was another propaganda film made by a company called The Emperor's Clothes which repeated Mr. Deichman's allegations. That's what you relied on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only on that. The allegation in The Emperor's Cloths should be seen here in Court if they haven't been. You should compare that film with the one we just saw. Secondly, if there was any clue that those -- they were very convincing. If there was any clue that they had manufactured that, it would certainly turn up in the discussion of this whole issue. And to sort of support the Dutch here, if it had come to the point where the whole allegation made by The Emperor's Clothes film had just been simply thought up, the Dutch would have reported it for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand -- I'm sorry, Professor. Do you understand, and we do have a copy and we can play it if you insist, that that film reported the allegations made by this German journalist or whatever he was called Deichman? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that Dr. Deichman -- I'm not sure he's a doctor -- but Deichman gave evidence at the libel trial?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume he probably had to, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you understand that this allegation, and indeed it can be clearly seen from the film itself, is an utterly false allegation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it from the film. And maybe someone else can. I'm not denying that you could be correct. It's just that on the basis of -- I'm trying to defend my research techniques, and that is viewing the film would not have helped me, I can assure you, to determine that point. What would have helped me would have been an open statement in the press and in the reliable accounts of the war and the propaganda on the war that that very detailed analysis of how this picture was taken was completely false. I never had any clue that anyone was denying this, and I don't see it here either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question on this: You knew that a libel trial had taken place?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fact, yes, after the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than The Emperor's Clothes and other than the part of the Dutch report which merely reported the controversy, did you make any effort to find out what had happened?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you I did not because we felt confident that if The Emperor's Clothes version about who was inside and outside that wire had been challenged, I would have run across it. I had no -- I would have certainly used that material if I'd had the opportunity, but we still don't know, do we? We still don't know. I've not received any kind of clear answer from anyone what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I suggest this to you, Professor Shoup, that when you leave this Court, you get hold, and indeed we'll provide you with a copy ourselves of the full transcript of the libel trial and it will show you beyond any venture that Mr. Deichman when he made these allegations was in error.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: About this particular point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About the fact that he alleged that ITV, ITN had deliberately faked footage. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that at all. You're still not answering -- I'm sorry. The question as to whether the man was inside or outside the barbed wire, but I would be delighted if you would -- I don't want to say that I'm always right. I would be delighted. I hope you will give me a copy of the transcript of the trial. I would be delighted to receive it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not really on the opposite side on this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor Shoup, I'm going to suggest to you finally that this whole report is full of errors because you haven't done insufficient -- you have done insufficient checking?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That means that you're really -- you're telling me the CIA is full of errors, you're telling me that the Dutch are full of errors, and you're telling me that the book is full of errors, on which I base most of this report. In other words, it's not simply the report itself, it's everything on which the report is based. If you would tell me that the report deviates from the book, if you would tell me that the report deviates from the Dutch study or the CIA study, I think that would be a very serious accusation. But it doesn't deviate from these studies; in effect, you're condemning all of the professional work that goes on, on this war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, Professor. What I'm suggesting is that the "Balkan Battlegrounds" and the NWID report suffer from the same problem that you do, which is that you have not had, for whatever reason in your case, access to the original documents.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is a startling assertion. Of course, original documents in this Court will help clarify what's in the book or what is in the Dutch report. But you're, in effect, saying that the Dutch should not try to do what they did, that they should not try to rely, for example, on the efforts of the United Nations Commission of experts which they quote, that they should not rely on the immense, immense efforts to try to describe the battles that went on in Bosnia that was done by the CIA. Why? Because you say that they are quotes secondary sources and not original sources. I am telling you over and over again when it comes to certain aspects of this situation, you need to analyse this material and present it to the rest of us. Now, take the International Red Cross, for example, are you saying that their reports are not to be relied on? I'm sorry, I can't ask you that question. But we have to rely on careful work done by international agencies, by people like the Dutch, for example, and then we have to supplement it with original documents that are now appearing here in the Court. I'm delighted to see these documents. I want to read them. We may change our opinions on certain aspects of the war. But I don't think that as of this moment you have challenged the veracity of this book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second aspect that I'm to suggest to you, Professor Shoup, and I think it's only right you should deal with it --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that you start with a bias and you have looked only for information that helps support your bias, namely that the Serbs have been unjustly blamed.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I shall answer that. If the Court has looked at this book, they will make their -- draw their own conclusions, and you will draw your own conclusions as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One, one --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the report that you wrote, Professor Shoup. This report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you an example of why I feel that this is an unjust accusation. Take the question of Karadzic's famous remarks of October 15th, 1991 when he said that the Muslims face annihilation. And we understand each other, don't we? It would have been very easy for me to note that Karadzic ended his remarks with the statement that we all face annihilation, and not note in the footnote that he said that after a pause in which the assembly erupted in scandalous discussions. Now, to the add to the irony of this charge that you're making, that observation as I remembered later, came from the BBC film which you challenged me to look at as though I had never seen it. In fact, that was precisely the source, although I had not remembered it at the time, where I -- where that footnote came from. Secondly, let's take the events we have just described. You're making a very serious accusation against my reputation. And I apologise to the Court if I don't follow the Judges' instructions, but I think I have to defend myself. Take the events in Trnopolje. I've made it very clear in the report that those persons who are at Trnopolje, many of them had come from Manjaca and other places where they had been mistreated. The irony of the film that we have been discussing is that when the British team came to the really bad places, as you know, Omarska and so forth, they were -- the inmates were not able to describe these terrible conditions. They were sort of shoved off. There was a terrible problem there. And I've not hidden it in the report. Some of these people were then at Trnopolje when the BBC group came. The point I was trying to make was that the international press picked up the picture of this gaunt figure behind barbed wire. As we know, that picture went throughout the world, and that was the end of the discussion. That's a concentration camp; nobody went into the details of this matter. That was taken for granted that that was all at stake. This is the point I was trying to make. But you must find many examples throughout this report as I think the Judges will see of my making clear that I'm not playing any favorites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're getting close to the end. I want to try to go rapidly because I have a lot to cover in a very short time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there will be questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We may not even finish today, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know that there's much choice. I mean, there's -- we've taken until leaving me 20 minutes and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have no intention of curtailing on your time, Mr. Ackerman. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's start, and maybe we can get finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe we'll stay for the day here. When were you scheduled to fly back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can go rapidly through what I was going to discuss first, Your Honour. I have -- I wanted to talk about the review of the movie that was done by this Joshua Tanzer. Since that came up in the cross-examination by Ms. Korner, we've done a little bit of research on this man, and I've given the document that we developed to Ms. Korner. And if Ms. Korner would simply agree that she was mistaken when she suggested that he was a reviewer for the New York Times, I won't ask any more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will. I have been shown I made an error because I can see from this he wrote headlines in the New York Post, and I'm afraid American newspapers are much the same to me. So I absolutely withdraw that he was with the New York Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit DB377. And we'll have to give it to the usher. I think it's here. And again, this is a document that I received actually from Ms. Korner, so this won't come as a surprise to anyone either. This, Your Honours, is the review that actually was written in the New York Times by one Steven Holden who is a film reviewer for the New York Times. And it's his review of "Yugoslavia, the Avoidable War."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it there, Professor Shoup?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only want to refer to a couple parts of it, if you go to the second page: "Whether or not you're convinced by the film assertions many of which are based on information provided by the Red Cross, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and other organisations that investigated reported events after the fact, "Yugoslavia, the Avoidable War", does an impressive job of relating the complicated history of the war and of filling in the background." And the last -- next -- right next to the last paragraph: "Has the meticulously chronological account of the Balkan Wars unfolds event by event, failed peace initiative by failed peace initial, "Yugoslavia, the Avoidable War" leads you to a no-man's land of doubt." Do you think those two paragraphs at least are fair reviews of that film?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be very careful in stating my view. I think that's it's important that people see films which have information that they might not have otherwise obtained. This film does have that kind of information. For example, the testimony of people like Lord Carrington, people might not have realised that he was against the recognition of Croatia. The fact that Dubrovnik was not destroyed is true, and it should be shown there. I cannot, in all honesty, agree with this meticulously chronological account of the Balkan wars, if you'll excuse me, because really I gave you the example to the Prosecutor a day or two ago of the events in Mostar in which things were compacted in such a way that you were led to believe chronologically that the Serbs had been the victims of mass liquidation in Mostar, and I thought that was really disinformation, if you will pardon me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but the idea that you have to look at such films and understand that some of these things are terribly important for you is my way of -- I just think this is terribly, terribly necessary. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, whether you're here tomorrow or not is in your hands. Just to warn you.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I'll be short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the film, you saw the -- you saw General Kukanjac, and you mentioned in your cross-examination that he had been in negotiations with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any agreement that they entered into regarding the withdrawal of troops, JNA troops from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be brief. I have been warned. There was an incident, of course, connected with the return of Izetbegovic from abroad, May 1st and 2nd, in which Izetbegovic was held by the JNA. There were negotiations with General MacKenzie. Part of the agreement I think was that the JNA should be permitted to leave at that particular point. MacKenzie thought everything was settled. When the JNA began to leave, the convoy was attacked, and MacKenzie was furious. If that's the incident you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was anybody killed in that attack on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I don't remember how many. But it was a betrayal of the United Nations, as MacKenzie saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And attacked by whom; do you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke also about the newspaper Oslobodjenje.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oslobodjenje, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you talked about how Oslobodjenje was a very reliable source. Did it remain reliable throughout the war? In other words, was it a reliable source in 1993, or did its character change in some way?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's character changed radically. It was a marvelous newspaper before the war. I made great efforts to obtain copies of the Oslobodjenje during the war from Zulfikarpasic in Zurich. He supplied me with these copies, and it turned out that Oslobodjenje during the war -- I wouldn't say it was propaganda, but it was -- it practically no information whatsoever of any use to a person studying the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think I have just one more question. Ms. Korner was asking you about the issue of self-defense, were the Muslims engaged in self-defense, were the Serbs engaged in self-defense.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just very lightly mentioned Mostar and Konjic. Are you familiar with the events that took place in Konjic in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the persecution both of the Croats and the Serbs during that period by the Muslims in Konjic. In the book, I think we mention this. And that actually there was an investigation of this situation by Sarajevo which didn't change events very much. I won't say more than that because I would have to refresh my memory about the exact details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that the Muslim forces were engaged in self-defense in --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Activities they undertook in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Let's be careful about this. All sides were trying to be sure that the other sides didn't take advantage of the situation. The Muslims put Serbs and Croats in camps where they would be no threat to them. Maltreated them. I see that action as being absolutely the equivalent of what was taking place in the north, perhaps on a somewhat smaller scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Professor. Thank you so much for coming and trying to help us. And I wonder if the Prosecution could remember to return his "Balkan Battlegrounds" book before he leaves. Otherwise, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, do you have any questions, Judge Janu? We have some questions for you. Judge Janu from the Czech Republic will go first. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Am I right, Professor, if I presuppose that you can speak Serbo-Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: How long -- how many years did you spend in former Yugoslavia, altogether? We can start that we know from your CV that you read law in University of Belgrade. So how many years was study and other years spent in former Yugoslavia or the south Yugoslavia altogether?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to think a minute. I would say that I was there with a leave of absence from my university for full time for maybe two or three years. And then I would go back to Yugoslavia every summer or spring for two or three months over a period of 20 years. So I would imagine, really, we're talking about ten years, 15 years maybe all told if I put all of this together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And study itself was how many years?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Study took a long time. Professor Burg at one point could not finish his part of the book, so that we stopped --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We ended the research in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: No, Professor. I am back at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That you told us that you studied the law faculty of Belgrade. How long this study --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. This was the first exchange between the United States and Yugoslavia. It was very -- it was very much at the very beginning; Stalin was still alive, for example. The three of us, none of us knew Serbo-Croatian. We were sent there as a sort of pioneer effort so that our first job was to learn the language, and this is what we tried to do. But I -- in the end, we all decided that the best thing to do was to be a student, to try to absorb the culture. And in the end, I did not take a degree or attend more than a few lectures at the law faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. The video we saw here before the break, there was a speech of Minister Ostojic, and he said something like the religious war which has been inflicted upon the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My question is, what in your view and in your experience was the role of the orthodox church in the conflict, or maybe other churches as well? If you are able to --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. The orthodox church took a nationalist position and helped, I'm afraid, to -- and contributed to the tensions in Bosnia by doing so. When it -- the Catholic church, on the contrary, was a force for reconciliation among the various ethnic groups. And Ostojic's effort to say that somehow the Vatican was behind all of this, you may have noticed that, I think is just pure imagination. When it comes to the Islamic community, we have to -- it's more difficult to say. The expert, Mr. Xavier Bougarel, a French specialist, describes in detail the fact that within the SDA there were both more fundamentalist groups who foresaw that Bosnia might become a totally Islamic state, and there are more secularly minded persons who wanted sincerely to create some kind of a Balkan civil society.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. On the page 14 of your report, you said something like this: That there were two events during the course of 1990, and that events were crucial and highly detrimental for the future of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: The first one, and I was like to stay with the first one, first was the breakup of the Yugoslav League of Communists in January 1990.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So, Professor, you said you were in former Yugoslavia when Tito still was in power. So you know that his relationship with Stalin at the beginning was very close --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And that his socialistic steps in Yugoslavia were very, very resolute. His collectivisation was maybe more stricter than in the former Soviet Union, and change became afterwards.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So you are aware of this. My question is, how you can say that breakdown of communist system was highly detrimental? We know that breakup of communist was in whole central and east Europe, and it was beneficial in all the ways. So I would like to put to you wasn't it more the not old communist leaders who were not able, because of their past, to be successful in the peaceful transformation of the country than this --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps these two positions are complementary rather than being contradictory. The old communist leaders of Bosnia had an opportunity to try to keep Bosnia from falling into ethnic chaos. And they were not able to do so. And I won't go into a lengthy description of why, except to say that I think that by 1990 the communist party of Bosnia had been paralysed by infighting, you know, among these people. They bear a responsibility. But they were under pressure from what was happening in the rest of Eastern Europe to hold free elections, and what was happening in the rest of Yugoslavia. And they gave way to that pressure, and the consequences were those that we saw. Three nationalist parties locked in combat with one another. The transition itself was rocky in Bosnia, much more so than in the Czech Republic, for example, simply because it resembled more the transition in some of these eastern countries such as the Ukraine or Moldavia or whatever. A sudden total transformation. There had been no dissident movement in Bosnia, as in the Czech Republic, to which people could turn. So it went from communism to nationalism, just like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. My last question is what's your opinion about the Islamic Declaration which was, as you remind us here --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: -- reprinted 1990?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the book, I treat it very cautiously. I mention -- I, we, Professor Burg and I mention it but pass on because this was an object of a great deal of propaganda on all sides. People -- the Serbs were saying look what he proposes here, and let's -- how could we possibly live in such a state? My conclusions now are that the Islamic Declaration was important not for what it said, but because it was used by the SDA before the elections widely, according to Xavier Bougarel the expert on this, and in other words, the Muslims were waving copies of this document. And in other words, it was being brought up to date. Izetbegovic would say, no, this is past. That was 20 years ago. But in fact, there were those who were on the Muslim side who were using this document as a way of trying to get people to vote for their party. That brings it right up to the time of the elections. As far as the contents is concerned, I think -- I'll be quick -- I think if I was reading it I would conclude that when the Muslims were to become a majority in Bosnia, they would then wish to impose some kind of an Islamic culture and political system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Janu. Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: On page 18 of your report, in the middle of this page, you said that the debate over plans to hold a referendum for independence which took place on January 25th, 1992, also ended with a walkout of the SDS. This was a critical moment. Bosnia was poised on the brink of war.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The Bosnian parliament seemed ready to consider Serb demands for the regionalisation of Bosnia as a condition for holding a referendum for independence only to be blocked by Izetbegovic. My question is as follows: Is it correct to say that this Serb demand is Bosnia-Herzegovina should maintain confederation with federal Yugoslavia, or so it becomes independent state on the basis of three ethnic regions?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. This debate does not concern the question of a confederal relationship with Serbia or Croatia or the other members of the former Yugoslavia, but whether a referendum which will declare Bosnia an independent state should first be preceded by some agreement between the three ethnic communities over what that state should look like. In other words, would it be made up of national cantons or whatever. There is a certain presumption here that it would have made sense to try to first decide how Bosnia was to look before you then went ahead and declared its independence. Maybe I haven't completely understood the question. I do beg your patience and indulgence. If you wish to clarify this, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: What is the difference of this Serb demand from the Lisbon Accord?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no -- well, the Lisbon Accords come later. And in effect, the Lisbon Accords are trying to spell out what that constitutional settlement accompanying independence might look like. And as we noted, the Lisbon Accords were very brief. They didn't go into great detail, but they seemed to supply the notion of national cantons which for the Serbs was what they wanted at this particular moment. And at the same time, the Lisbon Accords affirmed the independence of Bosnia. So in effect, they were trying to wrap up what had happened, providing the constitutional settlement that had not been provided in the Assembly, and at the same time acknowledging that Bosnia was independent, which the referendum had done. So that the Lisbon Accords were bringing both of these points together into one package, as it were. And as we know, Karadzic, for his own reasons, accepted this. Izetbegovic did not. But I don't believe that Karadzic was entirely sincere either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said in your report, on this paragraph, this Serb demand was only to be blocked by Izetbegovic. How was the general attitude of Muslim population vis-a-vis an idea of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Judge Taya. He has got a problem with his earpiece.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could somebody give me the transcript button? There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, can you just switch on his monitor on transcript mode so he can read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. Here we are. Let's see. All right. You asked what was the general attitude of the Muslim population vis-a-vis the idea of national cantons, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they were suspicious. I think they felt that the national cantons would be dominated by the Serbs, and I think that suspicion was justified. On the other hand, everybody -- the average person wants to avoid a war. This is the point. They are desperate to avoid a war, I think. And in that context, if I was to ask a Muslim at this stage would you accept national cantons, many of them might have said, if the option -- if the alternative is war, yes, I would, reluctantly, but I would. But this is just hypothetical. You can see that they were in a terrible, terrible dilemma at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to have to go back and ask permission to read the cross, but perhaps I could ask what he's basing this on, what evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's speculating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's speculating on the assumption that everyone would do practically -- and accept practically everything to avoid war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. I'm sorry. That's why I rose to my feet. It really is important if we're going to have these general statements, that we know what he's basing them on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was being perceived as a speculation, at least from my point of view in any case. Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Do you know that part that on 9th January 1992 Assembly of Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted the creation on the proclamation of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina being part of federal Yugoslav state, and that the territory of that state includes even the regions in which the Serbian people remained in the minority due to the genocide conducted against it in World War II.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the question, if you'll be patient for a moment. I have to use the transcript here. Yes, I think I understand the question now. You're referring to this area of Bosanska Krajina, and you're referring to the charge that was made by the Serbians -- by the Serbs that the only reason that they had to act to incorporate areas such as Sanski Most into this ARK was that it was truly Serb because the people there -- because the Serbs had been -- so many Serbs had died during World War II. Therefore, they had the right to include this area in the ARK. Is this what we're after? I'm sorry. I don't like those kinds of claims. I think that they can be -- you can go as far back in history as you wish to justify your claims to a certain piece of territory. I don't think this is sincere. I mean, it is sincere, but not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But you know the fact?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts are correct, that is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I assist. I think that the witness and Her Honour are at cross-purposes. She was asking about the declaration of the Serbian republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nothing to do with the autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether the professor was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware. I'm sorry. I don't like those claims that are based on history, Your Honour. I think that these are self-serving, and maybe that's -- I've said enough. Yes. I don't like them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But you are not aware of the declaration adopted by the Assembly of Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina on 9th January 1992?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Taya. Judge Taya is from Japan. I forgot to tell you that in the beginning. I would have loved to put a few questions to you, but if I were to put all the questions that I would like to, then that would mean you will have to stay here tomorrow. So I think I will skip questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I assist, I'm not sure there's another case in the Court this afternoon. There isn't, so it may be with a short break, that the interpreters may let --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply concerned. I don't want Your Honour to go away feeling there are questions you'd like to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can live without asking the questions, Ms. Korner, believe me. Otherwise I would have certainly -- there are a few issues mainly arising out of the report that on which I would prefer to tackle Professor Shoup. I think we can leave it at that. Professor, I should like to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber and also on behalf of the Tribunal for -- not only for having come here to give your expert testimony, but also for the way in which you testified. You have refocussed some of the spotlights we had already on and switched on others which, of course, is food for thought for us, the three Judges presiding over this case. We can assure you that everything that you said will be taken -- will be given due weight, due consideration by us in our deliberations. You will receive all the assistance you require after you are ushered out of the courtroom to enable you to return home. And on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya, and of course myself, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your courteous treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour, I'd like for Dr. Shoup to meet us in the lobby so I can return some documents to him. And second of all, his report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- unless it's a problem with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're finished now. His report is being tendered as Defence Exhibit DB376.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Made the registry happy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We haven't got time today, but Mr. Ackerman produced a whole list of exhibits, not all of which have been put in. But in any event, I will be submitting to Your Honour that the majority should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That we'll deal with on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's Wednesday afternoon, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is definitely in the afternoon because I have got meetings in the morning. So that's why the sitting is in the afternoon. Okay. Usher, please escort Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I wish to publicly thank the interpreters, the technicians, and the rest of the staff for having indulged us for about 10 minutes, 12 minutes over and above the normal schedule. I apologise to you if I did not try to seek your permission before, but I anticipated the sitting not to go beyond what it has actually gone. So I thank you once more publicly because without your cooperation, Professor Shoup would have had to return here tomorrow morning. Thank you. And good afternoon to everyone. We'll meet again on Wednesday in the afternoon. Thank you. If you can shift it to the morning, try. Thank you.
